summary.value: ProofBridge is a unified framework for directly translating both the statement and proof from natural to formal language. It utilizes an embedding system that projects FL and NL statements to a joint space. This is used as a retriever for the autoformalization model which the authors train using SFT. The model is tested with iterative repair and it demonstrates superior performance in type check rate and semantic correctness compared to baselines.

strengths.value:
The task of end-to-end proof autoformalization has, as the authors claim, been underexplored and it is an interesting new problem formulation. It is well-motivated by the difficulty manual formalization, such as during the AlphaProof experiment on IMO 2024 problems. Although there has been existing work on statement or proof autoformalization, an end-to-end approach for both statements and proofs has rarely been explored or evaluated. The experiment results rigorously show the proposed method's advantage over the numerous baselines considered. This paper may serve as a solid baseline for this end-to-end autoformalization setting for the community.

The presentation of this paper is clear and easy to follow.

weaknesses.value:
My biggest concern is that while the problem setting has been underexplored, the method that the authors consider is largely only piecing together existing approaches. The method largely resembles existing work on retrieval-augmented statement autoformalization (see below), with the added complexity that it starts training from Kimina-Prover-1.7B which has been trained for proving already.

Contrary to what the authors claim, I think NL/FL joint embedding has been explored in previous work, in the form of first informalizing the FL statement and then embedding NL queries and informalized theorems into a joint space, and retrieving similar FL examples from NL queries at test time for the purpose of statement or proof autoformalization. This was proposed in prior work like [1, 2, 3]. In this paper, the authors proposed a slightly different method that trains linear projections from FL and NL embeddings (based on existing models) into a shared space. Although technically different, I don't see how this is advantageous compared to existing approaches based on informalization which have shown to be effective. Either some explanation or quantitative comparison is needed to demonstrate this.

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.13310v2
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10878
[3] https://openreview.net/forum?id=hUb2At2DsQ

The "Semantic Correctness" (SC) evaluation metric is not new. In [1], the BEq metric was introduced which is basically the same as SC. Subsequent work such as RLMEval [2] and StepFun-Formalizer [3] have extended and improved BEq (although I admit the latter should be considered contemporaneous work). Even ignoring BEq, there has been extensive prior work on using an LLM judge as a semantic correctness check. This is a small issue, but I would encourage the authors to recognize the previous work.

[1] https://openreview.net/forum?id=hUb2At2DsQ
[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07222
[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.04440

The retriever baseline, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, shouldn't be considered a SOTA. That is a small model pretrained on general NL data. I encourage the authors to try a larger pretrained model such as e5-mistral-7b-instruct (which LeanSearch seems to use), or at least not label the current baseline as SOTA (because LeanSearch exists).

questions.value: For the same natural language problem, there might exist different correct ways to state it in Lean, some being easier to prove than others. Do the authors envision ProofBridge to be extensible to optimize for downstream provability of formalized statements?

In contrast, ProofBridge uses a DAG-aware FL encoder and a contrastive joint NL-FL embedding that captures proof structure, leading to significantly better separation in embedding space and higher Recall and MRR for NL-to-FL theorem+proof retrieval, which enables effective retrieval-augmented SFT for proof auto-formalization. **_[W3] The "Semantic Correctness" (SC) evaluation metric is not new. In [1], the BEq metric was introduced ... basically the same as SC. Subsequent work such as RLMEval [2] and StepFun-Formalizer [3] have extended and improved BEq … would encourage the authors to recognize the previous work._**

We thank the reviewer for pointing out BEq and related prior work on semantic correctness metrics. We have incorporated the reviewer’s feedback in the **revised submission** by adding the relevant citations and discussing key differences between them and our Semantic Correctness (SC) metric (_Section A.4 in the Appendix_).

While the general idea behind our SC metric and BEq[1,3] is similar, as both aim to establish bidirectional equivalence in Lean, the sets of allowed tactics differ. Since the notion of equivalence depends on the permitted tactics, these differences lead to meaningful distinctions between SC and BEq. BEq+[2] is a reference-based metric inspired by BEq. However, BEq+ is deterministic and CPU-efficient, while SC relies on an LLM-based proof synthesizer. This creates a trade-off: the LLM judge can capture equivalences beyond the reach of the deterministic procedure, whereas BEq+ provides a reproducible evaluation.

To illustrate the difference between our SC metric and BEq, we refer the reviewer to the example provided in **Appendix A.4** (_page 16_). In the appendix example, the two propositions differ primarily in the use of an auxiliary variable (v): 

- Proposition 1 (gold-standard FL theorem from miniF2F-Test-PF) explicitly introduces an auxiliary variable v to denote volume.

- Proposition 2 (produced by Kimina-Prover-RL-1.7B) omits the auxiliary variable and substitutes the corresponding formula directly.

To the best of our understanding of BEq as presented in the paper[1], these propositions would not be recognized as equivalent under the tactic set permitted by BEq. Our SC metric, by contrast, was specifically designed to handle such forms of equivalence. Variations like this occur frequently in practice, and human experts themselves often differ in whether they prefer introducing auxiliary variables. By explicitly handling these variations and using LLM-generated bidirectional proofs that are type-checked, SC provides an evaluation that is both more lenient in accepting semantically equivalent variations and more faithful in assessing the performance of autoformalization models.

Further, we have added a **qualitative example** in _Appendix A.5_ of the revised submission. The example presents an NL theorem and proof pair from miniF2F-Test-PF, showing: (i) the pass@1 proof auto-formalization output from Kimina-Prover-RL-1.7B in the text-based retrieval few-shot setting, which is type-correct but not semantically correct, (ii) the retrieved semantically relevant formal Lean theorem and proof pairs from our database, and (iii) the pass@1 proof auto-formalization output from ProofBridge, which is both type-correct and semantically correct (along with the proof of bi-directional equivalence to the gold-standard theorem).

summary.value: This paper presents a framework for automatically translating natural language mathematical theorems and proofs into Lean 4 formal language with RAG. The approach consists of three main components: (1) a joint embedding model that aligns natural and formal language theorem-proof pairs, (2) retrieval-augmented fine-tuning of LLMs, and (3) an iterative repair mechanism that uses Lean's type checker and semantic equivalence verification. The authors demonstrate improvements over baselines on some experiments.

strengths.value:
1. The use of LeanDojo’s ByT5 encoder to capture the "linearized DAG traversal" of Lean proofs, rather than just treating the code as flat text. It might be a thoughtful method for encoding the structural properties of formal proofs.
2. The integration of RAG and SFT is well-executed. The authors provide corresponding ablation studies which help demonstrate the impact of SFT.

weaknesses.value:
1. The core motivation of the task, i.e., translating a known natural language proof into a formal proof, is questionable. The primary value of formal math languages is to verify statements whose correctness is uncertain. In most practical scenarios, a formal statement is the starting point, and the proof is the unknown to be found. If an informal proof is already known to be correct, the motivation for formalization becomes unclear. Of course, you can state that it's useful in some scenarios, like translating textbooks and formalizing existing proofs. But currently, what you are claiming is that the previous 2-stage practice (formalize statement and prove in formal language) is problematic, and yours is correct. It's not the case.
2. The paper claims the superiority of encoding the "linearized DAG traversal" using the ByT5 encoder. However, there is no ablation study to support this. How does this compare to a simpler baseline, such as encoding the raw text of the FL proof?
3. The experimental comparisons in Table 2 are insufficient and potentially misleading: (1) The baseline models were also provided with the full input context, i.e., the NL theorem, the NL proof, and retrieved RAG examples, right? Then the authors should provide ablations that isolate the benefit of the (arguably unrealistic) input. Specifically, how much does adding the NL proof and the RAG component each contribute to the performance of both the baseline and the proposed model? This is crucial to understand if PROOFBRIDGE is genuinely better at using the informal proof, or whatever else. (2) The reported Semantic Correctness for powerful models like Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5-mini seems anomalously low. The authors should provide a case study or a deeper analysis explaining these failures. (3) The paper dismisses Kimina-Autoformalizer for achieving 0% correctness. This is a strawman argument. These models are designed for statement formalization only and to output sorry, not end-to-end proof generation. Stating they "perform poorly" is an unfair characterization of models built for a different task.
4. The work is missing a comparison to REAL-Prover: Retrieval Augmented Lean Prover for Mathematical Reasoning (arXiv:2505.20613, 2025), which is highly relevant to this work.

**_[W1] The core motivation of the task, i.e., translating a known natural language proof into a formal proof, is questionable…In most practical scenarios, a formal statement is the starting point, and the proof is the unknown to be found…If an informal proof is already known to be correct, the motivation for formalization becomes unclear…_**

We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this concern. We respectfully disagree with the assertion that translating natural language (NL) proofs to formal language (FL) proofs is of limited value. Our clarification of the motivation for proof auto-formalization is as follows:

- **NL proofs are never guaranteed to be perfectly correct due to their inherent ambiguity.** By definition, any proof written in NL is ambiguous; it can contain subtle errors or hidden assumptions, even when it appears detailed. As discussed in the Introduction (Section 1), many historical counterexamples illustrate this, including cases where seemingly correct NL proofs were later found to contain non-trivial errors. Only by formalizing NL proofs into languages such as Lean, Isabelle, or Coq, each with strict syntax and symbolic logic, can we achieve reliable automated verification guarantees. Thus, the process of proof auto-formalization resolves the inherent ambiguity of NL proofs via computer-verifiable FL proofs.

- **Proof discovery is a separate problem; in practical scenarios, efficient FL proof synthesis relies on guidance from NL proofs or proof sketches.** We respectfully note that our work focuses on proof auto-formalization, not on proof discovery. Proof discovery is a distinct problem: given an FL theorem, the goal is to generate a correct FL proof without any guidance, as for some open problems even mathematicians may not know how the proof should proceed. In such cases, the tool must search blindly (inefficiently or using heuristics) over a vast space of tactics.

    However, for the majority of mathematical problems, humans typically have an idea of the proof in NL, or at least a proof sketch, though its correctness is not guaranteed until it is formalized. Proof auto-formalization leverages this guidance, accelerating FL proof construction and helping uncover hidden errors in the NL proof or sketch. In practice, almost all human formalization efforts, such as in Lean, Isabelle, or Coq, begin by assuming the NL proof is correct and validate it through translation to FL. Attempting to generate FL proofs “from nothing” is rarely practical; using NL proofs as a starting point is both realistic and essential for efficient formalization. This approach underlies interactive theorem proving (ITP), where humans provide strategies and the system verifies them.

    Lastly, starting from an FL theorem necessitates human hand-formalization of the NL theorem, which impedes a fully automated formalization pipeline.

- **NL proofs provide valuable structural guidance, even if imperfect or incomplete.** Even if an NL proof contains minor errors, it can still be highly useful for a proof auto-formalization tool in planning the structure of the corresponding FL proof, for example, indicating whether induction, case analysis, or proof by contradiction should be applied. In the rare case where an NL proof is completely incorrect, auto-formalization may fail. Similar failures can also occur in proof discovery when no guidance is provided. These cases highlight an opportunity for future research: analyzing whether the failure arises from limitations of the prover or flaws in the NL proof itself. The ability to validate and refine the correctness of arbitrary NL proofs is made possible only through proof auto-formalization.

Overall, we believe that a system translating NL theorem-proof pairs into FL is far more practical and usable than hand-formalizing the theorem first, and then relying on proof discovery, particularly when humans can provide guidance through an NL proof sketch. Importantly, we are not claiming that the traditional two-stage approach of “formalize the statement, then search for a formal proof from scratch” is invalid or problematic. Rather, we argue that leveraging NL proof guidance provides a complementary and often highly effective signal, especially for complex problems where formal proof search alone may be insufficient. Our framework is designed to augment existing theorem-proving approaches, not replace them.

------

The low SC of foundation models such as Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5-mini can be attributed to several factors. Although these models excel at NL generation, they are not trained to strictly adhere to the syntactic and semantic rules of specialized formal languages (FLs) like Lean. Producing a valid formal proof requires precise handling of proof tactics, dependency graphs, and formal logic structures, which are often underrepresented or absent in the models’ pretraining corpora. When formalizing NL proofs from miniF2F-Test-PF, Gemini-2.5-Pro frequently generated sequences superficially resembling Lean syntax but with mismatched tactics, missing arguments, or invalid references to definitions. GPT-5-mini often produced syntactically invalid Lean tokens and violated key dependencies in the proof DAG, resulting in verification failures. These demonstrate that even powerful LLMs cannot reliably perform AFPS or full proof auto-formalization out-of-the-box. As reflected in _Table 2_, these models’ TC accuracies are low, which directly limits SC, as semantic correctness requires type-correct proofs.

Because foundation models are not inherently effective for AFPS and auto-formalization in specialized FLs like Lean, several SoTA LLMs have been developed for these tasks. We list and compare many such tools in Section 5.3 and evaluate ProofBridge against them in _Table 1_ and _Section 5.5_.

We acknowledge that Kimina-Autoformalizer-7B and Herald-Translator are designed specifically for theorem (statement) auto-formalization. Our rationale for including these models is that, since our work addresses end-to-end auto-formalization (NL-to-FL), it is important to compare against available SoTA auto-formalization tools. Our results show that models focused solely on statement formalization are unsuitable for generating full FL proofs. Our method is compatible with such decomposition: each sub-goal lemma can be supported by the retrieval of semantically aligned NL-FL fragments, and the auto-formalizer operates over manageable pieces whose equivalence can still be checked via our SC metric.
